name: Tomas Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a call-out electrician for Keystone Facilities, a contractor that looks after a supermarket chain's stores and a few office blocks across the region. My phone buzzes, I get a job like a chiller tripping or the car park lights out, and I drive there and sort it before the store manager loses it. I like the puzzle of it, walking in cold and working out what's wrong in twenty minutes. What wears me out is the nights on standby, when you sleep with the phone on your chest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, how are things?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a rented studio by the ring road. I'm on the lower end of pay for this job, and rent eats nearly half of it, so I've got maybe three weeks saved. There aren't many electrician jobs in town that aren't with Keystone or the council. I play five-a-side on Thursdays, which is about my only luxury.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. So AI's a damp squib. Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, it was always oversold. At work we use a fault-finding chatbot on the tablet sometimes, and it's handy for looking up a chiller's wiring diagram, but that's it. Online I'd keep quiet, I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI was never my worry. Keystone's contract with the supermarket is up for tender next spring, and if a cheaper firm wins it, I either move over on their worse terms or I'm out. That's been on my mind for months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job well, because the store managers' reviews count at tender time. I'd start putting my CV together quietly, and ask the council's maintenance team if they've got anything coming up. And I'd cut the takeaway coffees, which is a silly amount every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. Not about robots, about April. It's like waiting for exam results you can't study for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is a silly amount on coffee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About twenty-five a week, if I'm honest, from the services on the bypass. That's a hundred a month I could be saving. I know, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the new firm took you on worse terms, what would you accept?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a bit less pay if the standby stayed the same. What I wouldn't take is a zero-hours call-out deal, where you only get paid when they ring. You can't pay rent on maybe.

say: I'd say AI was **always oversold**, and I'm not surprised.
I'd mention the **fault-finding chatbot** is handy for wiring diagrams, but that's it.
think: My real worry is the **supermarket contract**, up for tender next spring.
If a cheaper firm wins, I'd move on **worse terms** or lose the job.
do: Keep **store managers happy**, since their reviews count at tender.
Quietly update his **CV** and ask the council team about openings.
Cut **takeaway coffees**, about a hundred pounds a month.
feel: **Anxious** about the April tender, like waiting for exam results.
S0.quote: You can't pay rent on maybe.
fieldNote: His anxiety comes from **contract tendering**, not technology.
He uses AI **lightly**, for wiring diagrams, once colleagues had tried it.
He draws a clear line at **zero-hours** call-out work.
Living alone with **half his pay** on rent leaves little room for shocks.

steps.text: Keep store managers' reviews high before the tender
Ask the council maintenance team about openings
Stop buying coffee at the bypass services, saving a hundred monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and booking. That's our dispatch office, basically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a sensible change and people should get on board, but slowly. At work I'd say the dispatchers will have a hard time, they're mostly on the phones. To my mates I'd say sparks are fine, we're the hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it changes how I'm managed more than what I do. Software would send me jobs, plan my route, and probably track how long each one takes. That's fine until it decides I'm slow because I spent forty minutes on a fault the computer thinks is a ten-minute job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new dispatch app properly once it's on everyone's tablets, and I'd use the diagnosis bit more. I'd keep the CV going in case the tender goes badly. And I'd put the coffee money into savings, a hundred a month, to get to two months of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, because the tender's still there. The AI part makes me a bit uneasy, but I'll cope with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the software flagged you as slow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show my working, literally, with photos and notes from every job. And I'd ask the union rep to look at how the targets are set. I'm not against being measured, I'm against being measured by something that's never been in a chiller room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Keystone would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bev in dispatch. She's been there twelve years and she knows which store managers to call back first. If the software does her job, I hope they find her something, maybe in the stores team.

say: I'd call it a **sensible change**, best taken slowly.
I'd tell mates **electricians are the hands**, so we're fine.
think: Software would **send, route and time** my jobs, changing how I'm managed.
It could wrongly flag me as **slow** on faults it doesn't understand.
do: Learn the **dispatch app** properly once it's on everyone's tablet.
Keep the **CV** updated in case the tender goes badly.
Save the **coffee money**, a hundred a month, toward two months' rent.
feel: **Anxious** about the tender, and a bit **uneasy** about software management.
S1.quote: I'm not against being measured, I'm against being measured by something that's never been in a chiller room.
fieldNote: He sees AI changing **how he's managed**, not the work itself.
He'd defend himself with **evidence**, photos and notes, plus the union rep.
The **tender** remains his main source of anxiety.
His concern for the **dispatcher** shows he notices who gets hit first.

steps.text: Learn Keystone's new dispatch app once it's rolled out
Save a hundred a month toward two months' rent
Ask the union rep to review job-time targets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Robots by 2031. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is serious and the government needs to get a grip fast. At work I'd say keep calm, we've got a bit longer than the office people. I'd probably share a few sensible articles, nothing ranty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the supermarket is the problem. If AI runs the stores and the warehouses by 2028, they'll cut costs everywhere, and maintenance contracts are first. By 2031, a robot that can swap a chiller fan at three in the morning without overtime is exactly what the supermarket would want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the refrigeration and air conditioning course, because cooling systems are complicated and supermarkets can't live without them. I'd use AI for studying it, since it's good for that. And I'd look at moving to a bigger city where there are more firms, even though I'd lose the five-a-side lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, in a quiet way. I'd be thirty-two with no house, no savings and a trade a robot can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why move to a city when you've got friends here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because there are maybe four electrical firms in this town and fifty in the city. If robots take a third of the work, I'd rather be competing in a big pond. I'd miss Thursdays, though, a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you afford a move with three weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need a job lined up first, with a start date. Then I'd ask my dad for a loan for the deposit, which I'd hate. He'd say yes and then mention it at every Sunday dinner.

say: I'd say the **government** needs to get a grip fast.
I'd tell coworkers to **keep calm**, since we have longer than office staff.
think: An AI-run supermarket would **cut maintenance contracts** first.
By 2031 a **night-shift robot** without overtime is exactly what the supermarket would want.
do: Take the **refrigeration and air conditioning** course, using AI to study.
Look at **moving to a city** with more electrical firms.
Borrow a **deposit** from his dad only with a job lined up.
feel: **Quietly scared** at facing robots at thirty-two with nothing behind him.
S2.quote: By 2031, a robot that can swap a chiller fan at three in the morning without overtime is exactly what the supermarket would want.
fieldNote: He traces risk through his **client**, the supermarket, cutting costs.
Retraining into **refrigeration** is a practical, specialist move.
He'd **move cities** reluctantly, sacrificing his friends.
Help from his **dad** is available but unwelcome.

steps.text: Enrol on a refrigeration and air conditioning course
Apply for electrician jobs in the nearest big city
Use AI tutors to study refrigeration theory
Borrow a rental deposit from his dad once hired

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots three after. I'd be about thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming and we'd better plan, but there's time. At work I'd say get your extra tickets now. I'd probably say the same thing at five-a-side, where half the lads are in trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I can do this without panic. Refrigeration ticket in two years, then a move to a bigger firm. By 2034 I'd want to be the guy they call when the robot's broken, not the guy the robot replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the refrigeration course next September, at night school. I'd use the AI diagnosis tools at work more, so I'm comfortable with them by the time they're everywhere. And I'd build to two months of rent before I move anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. More focused than frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does being the guy they call when the robot's broken look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, really. Someone rings at three in the morning because the thing that does the job isn't doing the job. Only now the thing is a robot, not a chiller, and I'd need to know both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to fund night school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, maybe, if the bus timetable works. Definitely the coffee. Not the five-a-side, that's my sanity.

say: I'd say it's coming, we'd better plan, but **there's time**.
I'd urge tradespeople at five-a-side to get **extra tickets** now.
think: Five years lets me plan **without panic**: refrigeration ticket, then a bigger firm.
By 2034 I want to be **fixing the robots**, not replaced by them.
do: Start the **refrigeration course** at night school next September.
Use **AI diagnosis tools** more at work to get comfortable.
Build to **two months of rent** before moving anywhere.
S3.quote: By 2034 I'd want to be the guy they call when the robot's broken, not the guy the robot replaced.
fieldNote: Five years turns his fear into a **sequenced plan**.
His goal is **repair work** on robots, an extension of call-out work.
He protects **five-a-side** as his one fixed comfort.
Still anxious because of **thin savings** and the tender hanging over him.

steps.text: Start the refrigeration course at night school next September
Use AI diagnosis tools on every call-out
Save toward two months of rent before any move

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is manageable if people start early. At work I'd say there's a whole decade to get ready. I'd tell my dad not to worry, because he worries about this stuff from the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be nearly forty before robots arrive. That's a long time to get a better job, maybe buy a small place and have something behind me. The worry isn't 2039, it's still April and the tender.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the refrigeration ticket over three years. I'd try for a supervisor role at Keystone, or at whoever wins the contract. And I'd save steadily, aiming for three months by thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious, mainly about the near stuff. The far stuff feels like something I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to the tender. Why does it matter so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's real and it's six months away. AGI in ten years is a story, but losing my contract in April is a letter in my letterbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any bigger plans, like buying a home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still want to buy, maybe at thirty-two or thirty-three. But I'd want to see the robots coming first, so I don't buy a flat in a town with no work left.

say: I'd call it **manageable** if people start early, with a whole decade to get ready.
I'd reassure my **dad**, who worries about the stories he sees on the news.
think: At nearly forty when robots come, I'd have time for a **better job** and savings.
My real worry is still the **April tender**, not 2039.
do: Get the **refrigeration ticket** over three years.
Apply for a **supervisor role** with Keystone or the winning firm.
Save steadily toward **three months** by thirty.
feel: A bit **anxious** about near-term problems, but able to plan for the far ones.
S4.quote: AGI in ten years is a story, but losing my contract in April is a letter in my letterbox.
fieldNote: The **tender** dominates even when AGI is a decade off.
He'd **delay buying a home** until he sees where robots land.
A decade lets him aim for **promotion**, not just survival.
Anxious because thin savings and **contract risk** persist regardless of AI.

steps.text: Get the refrigeration ticket over three years
Apply for a supervisor role at Keystone
Save toward three months of expenses by age thirty
Delay buying a flat until the robot timeline is clearer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years is nothing when you've got three weeks of savings and a contract up for tender. What would help is cheap night-school courses for trades, and rules that stop contractors from moving everyone onto zero-hours call-outs when the work gets tight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about contracts. A lot of us don't work for the place we fix, we work for a contractor that can lose the job any year. That's a worry nobody sees from outside.

headlineQuote: A lot of us don't work for the place we fix, we work for a contractor that can lose the job any year.
portrait: Tomas is a **27-year-old call-out electrician** for a facilities contractor serving a supermarket chain and offices.
He lives alone in a rented studio, with **three weeks** of savings and rent eating half his pay.
He uses a **fault-finding chatbot** now and then, adopting tools after colleagues have tried them.
His constant worry is the **contract tender**, which colours every scenario more than AI does.
His plan is to add a **refrigeration ticket** and become the person who fixes robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because thin savings and a contract tender leave no room to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: Rules stopping contractors from forcing **zero-hours** call-out deals.
